newsitem.title: USA: Army drops more charges against sex-case sergeant.
newsitem.headline: Army drops more charges against sex-case sergeant.

text.p: The U.S. Army dropped 35 charges on Friday against a drill instructor accused of numerous counts of sexual misconduct involving female trainees at the scandal-plagued Aberdeen Proving Ground.

After a closed-door meeting between military prosecutors and attorneys for Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson, Simpson's attorneys said the charges, which included four counts of rape involving two women and two counts of forcible sodomy, had been dropped.

The action came a day after Army Trial Judge Col. Paul Johnston threw out 19 charges against Simpson based on federal sex abuse laws. Simpson is also charged with rape and sodomy under military laws for the same incidents, and his attorneys successfully argued those laws took precedence.

Simpson still faces 94 counts of sexual misconduct -- including charges he raped eight women -- and other violations in connection with an investigation into sexual harassment by proving ground trainers of female trainees.
Jury selection in his trial is to begin on Monday, with the trial set to start a week later.
"They're narrowing the battlefield," Simpson's attorney, Maj. Michael Sawyers said.
Defence attorney Capt. Edward Brady said: "We've been saying all along that the government has been piling on charges."
Attorneys have denied that Simpson commited rape. Brady said there was no physical evidence in the case and that the issue of Simpson's guilt would come down to whose story was most believable.
"It all goes down to 'he said-she said,'" Brady said.

The attorneys said nine counts of indecent acts had been dropped in the face of a defence challenge that the charges were already covered by more severe charges. Other counts were dropped at the instigation of prosecutors and the base commander.
Earlier Friday, Simpson took the witness stand to describe months of a regimented, shackled existence under maximum security detention while awaiting trial.

Simpson was testifying at a pre-trial hearing regarding a defence request to credit him with time served if he is convicted and sentenced. The lawyers are seeking five days of credit for every day served, based on what they said were overly harsh conditions for someone who had not gone to trial.

Simpson, sporting a dress uniform and smooth-shaven head, said that during seven months of pre-trial detention at the Quantico Military Brig in Quantico, Virgina, he had spent 22 hours a day in a 6-by-8 foot cell, where he was not allowed to lie down from his 5 a.m. wake-up call until 6 in the evening.
"You can sit in your chair. You can stand, you can walk in your cell. That's all, sir," Simpson said in sombre tones as he described his confinement.

Breaks away from his cell included brief periods of "sunshine call" in which he was allowed to stand or sit outside, and a one-hour television break three times a week, he said. He was required to wear shackles during such breaks.
He said he had not been allowed to see a chaplain for Easter or Christmas.

Prison commander Chief Warrant Officer James Hart testified that the conditions of Simpson's treatment were standard for a maximum-security detainee, and said high security was warranted because of the severity of charges against Simpson and because he was believed to be a flight risk.
Simpson had not exhibited any behaviour problems during his confinement, he said.
Before being brought to Aberdeen for the pre-trial hearings this week, Simpson had been held at Quantico from Sept. 11.

Simpson is the only soldier, among 10 from Aberdeen charged in the sexual misconduct scandal, to have been detained pending trial. Four of those cases have been resolved, and Simpson would be the first soldier charged in the scandal to go to trial.

On Sunday, a summary court martial will be conducted in the case of Pvt. Toni Moreland, who recanted statements made to investigators that she had had consesual sex with an instructor at Aberdeen. She is being charged with making a false statement.
